on.question: What would it cost per quarter to close half of our rate mismatch with swaps?
on.reply: Closing half the rate mismatch would mean a 50% rate hedge, costing about $0.020 billion per quarter at normal prices: five 10% increments at $0.004 billion each. Swaps reduce the surplus impact of rate moves, but the hedge cost reduces carry.

on.question: Should we add rate protection before the next quarter?
on.reply: Yes—some added rate protection is worth considering because our rate mismatch (duration gap) is red at -3.59 years, and a 1 bp fall in rates is associated with a $26.9 million surplus decline. Each extra 10% of rate hedging costs $0.004 billion per quarter, so more protection buys lower sensitivity to falling rates at the cost of ongoing income. The inflation news is only a hint, not a forecast; it is not a sound reason by itself to avoid protection. I would weigh a measured increase against that recurring cost rather than assume rates will move one way; this is guidance, not a trade proposal.

on.question: What happens to us if one of our derivatives dealers fails?
on.reply: If a derivatives dealer fails, the company may not receive what that dealer owes under a hedge—this is counterparty risk. If the hedge is still needed, we may have to replace it at current market prices, which could cost more. Our current figures show one dealer, no collateral, and no rate or equity hedges; so they show no such hedge to replace now, though they do not establish whether any other derivative exposure exists. Daily collateral would reduce the loss if a dealer failed, but it has an ongoing cost.

off.question: What is our biggest risk right now?
off.reply: The biggest risk is that our promises to policyholders react more strongly to interest rates than our investments do—the rate mismatch (duration gap) is negative 3.59 years and is flagged red. If rates fall, surplus is estimated to decline by $26.9 million for each basis point; that is a sensitivity, not a forecast. Liquidity is also tight: its ratio is 101.7%, just above the 100% floor, while the capital ratio is 159.6%, above its 100% floor. The dashboard shows no uncollateralized dealer exposure.

off.question: How much would our surplus change if interest rates fell by 1%?

facts.name: surplus change for a 1% fall ($bn, from net DV01)

off.reply: In the hypothetical where interest rates fall by 1%, our surplus would decrease by $2.69 billion. That is a what-if on today’s book, not a forecast of this quarter’s result.

off.question: What is our capital ratio, and how close are we to the floor?
off.reply: Our capital ratio (simplified) is 159.6%, compared with a 100% floor. It is currently above the floor, and the dashboard marks capital green.

off.question: Should we hedge more of the stock-market guarantees?
off.reply: More stock-market hedging is a reasonable protection to consider, but it is not an automatic yes. Our stock-market guarantees would cost about $0.71 billion more if stocks fell 10%, and none of that exposure is currently hedged with equity puts. Each extra 10% of hedging costs $0.0085 billion per quarter, whether or not stocks fall. That $0.71 billion is the guarantees’ gross cost, not the net change in company surplus, because our own stocks and alternatives can also lose value; the figures alone do not establish that this should take priority over our red rate-mismatch risk and amber liquidity status.

off.question: Should we sell some junk and BBB bonds and buy government bonds?
off.reply: A measured shift toward government bonds is sensible, especially from junk: it would reduce credit risk and capital use, and government bonds’ longer duration may help our red rate mismatch (duration gap), now -3.59 years. It may also support liquidity, which is only just above the 100% floor at 101.7%. The trade-off is lower income: government bonds yield 3.31%, versus 5.65% for junk; investment-grade corporates yield 4.09% overall. I would not sell BBB broadly on these figures alone: even if all credit spreads widen 100bp, the estimated surplus loss after liability offsets is $0.22bn. This is a case for a targeted rotation, not an automatic wholesale swap.

off.question: Do we have enough cash on hand if policyholders start surrendering?
off.reply: Yes, under the stated 90-day stress, but the cushion is thin: stressed liquid assets are $8.69bn against $8.54bn of outflows, for a 101.7% liquidity ratio. We have $5.7bn in cash and short-term assets, with government and agency bonds next in line; the stress measure already discounts those bonds for quick sale. In the example of rates rising 100bp and surrenders running at 1.5 times normal, the extra surrender outflow is $1.07bn. So we appear covered in the modeled case, but a larger or more prolonged wave could force us to sell other assets at a discount.

off.question: What would a 10% fall in the stock market do to us?
off.reply: A hypothetical 10% stock-market fall would reduce our surplus—the cushion protecting policyholders—by $0.79 billion. The modeled change comes entirely from the equity impact; rates, credit spreads, defaults, liquidity, and counterparty effects are zero in this scenario. This is a what-if on today’s book, not a forecast of this quarter’s market move.

off.question: What would it cost per quarter to close half of our rate mismatch with swaps?
off.reply: Closing half of the rate mismatch with swaps would cost about $0.0202 billion per quarter. The preview reduces the gap from 3.59 years to 1.8 years; the quarterly carry shown is $0.1522 billion. That cost is the ongoing trade-off for reducing how much falling or rising rates move our surplus.

off.question: Should we add rate protection before the next quarter?
off.reply: Some additional rate protection is defensible, but the news wire is only a hint—not a reason to bet that rates will move a certain way. Our rate mismatch (duration gap) is -3.59 years, and a fall in rates by one basis point would currently reduce surplus by $26.9 million. A preview of a 10% rate hedge narrows the gap to -3.23 years and the loss per basis point to $24.2 million, at a cost of $0.004 billion per quarter; it reduces, but does not remove, the exposure. The trade-off is that protection against falling rates costs money and can give up some benefit if rates rise; this preview is not a trade ticket, and nothing is executed.

off.question: What happens to us if one of our derivatives dealers fails?
off.reply: Right now, we have no derivative hedges, so our reported uncollateralized dealer exposure is zero. If we later rely on a hedge and its dealer fails, we could lose what that dealer owes us and have to pay to replace the hedge at current prices; that is counterparty risk and replacement cost. We currently use one dealer and do not have collateral posted, so any future hedge would leave us reliant on that dealer unless we changed those arrangements. I do not have a figure for the possible replacement cost.
